scenes.heading: 3D shapes and nets
scenes.sub: Unfold a box and see what's inside
scenes.say: Every cereal box starts life as a flat piece of cardboard. Let's learn how 3D shapes are built, how to count their parts, and how they unfold into nets.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cut a cereal box along its edges until it lies flat
scenes.science: That flat shape is the net: every face appears once
scenes.breaks: a real box has gluing flaps. A maths net has no flaps, just the faces joined edge to edge.
scenes.say: Take an empty cereal box and cut along some edges until it lies flat. That flat shape is its net. Fold it back up and you get the box again. A real box has extra flaps for glue, but a maths net is just the faces.

scenes.heading: Faces, edges, vertices
scenes.say: A face is a flat surface. An edge is a line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner. A cube has six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.

scenes.heading: Faces, edges and vertices
scenes.say: Here's a cube. First its edges, with the hidden ones dashed. Then the labels: a face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner. A cube has six faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.
scenes.caption: A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, a vertex is a corner. A cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.

scenes.heading: Prism vs pyramid
scenes.say: A prism is like a loaf of bread: two identical ends. With an n-sided base it has n plus two faces, two n vertices and three n edges. A pyramid has one base and a point on top called the apex. It has n plus one faces, n plus one vertices and two n edges.

scenes.heading: Euler's rule
scenes.say: Here's a brilliant check. For any polyhedron, faces plus vertices minus edges equals two. That's Euler's rule. For a cube: six plus eight minus twelve is two.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A hexagonal prism: find F, V and E, then check with Euler's rule.
scenes.say: A hexagonal prism. A hexagon has six sides. Faces: six plus two is eight. Vertices: two times six is twelve. Edges: three times six is eighteen. Check: eight plus twelve minus eighteen is two. It works!

scenes.heading: A net of a cube
notes: Fold the row of 4 into a loop
The top and bottom squares close it
scenes.say: Finally, a net. Six squares appear in a cross. Fold the row of four into a loop, then the square above and the one below close the top and bottom. Every face appears exactly once.
scenes.caption: A cross of six squares. Fold the row of 4 into a loop; the squares above and below close the top and bottom.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Count faces, edges and vertices. Prisms and pyramids have patterns you can use. Check with F plus V minus E equals two. And a cube has eleven different nets. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Quick recap. Count faces, edges and vertices. Prisms and pyramids have patterns. Check with F + V − E = 2. A cube has 11 different nets. Now try the practice questions!
